claims.claim: **HAE angioedema is non-pitting swelling without urticaria, itching or redness.**
claims.source_text: Angioedema in hereditary angioedema (HAE) is non-pitting swelling not associated with urticaria, itching or redness
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Life-threatening laryngeal oedema can occur at any age.**
claims.source_text: Life-threatening laryngeal oedema can occur at any age
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Every child diagnosed with HAE should have a personalised ASCIA HAE management plan** saying when and how to treat attacks.
claims.source_text: Children diagnosed with HAE should have a personalised ASCIA HAE management plan explaining when and how to treat attacks
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Antihistamines, corticosteroids and adrenaline have no role in HAE angioedema.** Early specific treatment improves outcomes.
claims.source_text: Early management of HAE attacks with specific treatments has been shown to improve outcomes, efficacy and quality of life. Antihistamines, corticosteroids and adrenaline have no role in the management of HAE related angioedema
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: HAE is autosomal dominant: **Type 1** is an absolute C1-INH deficiency (85% of cases), **Type 2** a functional one.
claims.source_text: HAE is a rare but potentially life-threatening autosomal dominant disorder due to absolute (HAE-C1-INH Type 1 -- 85% of cases) or functional (HAE-C1-INH Type 2) deficiency of C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Presentations:** cutaneous swelling of face, limbs (especially hands and feet) and genitals in over 90% · upper airway swelling (tongue, soft palate, larynx), which can be life-threatening · abdominal pain with nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, which can cause dehydration and collapse · a non-pruritic erythema marginatum rash in about one third.
claims.source_text: Cutaneous angioedema: over 90% develop non-pitting, non-pruritic swelling affecting face, limbs (especially hands and feet) and genitals … Upper airway swelling: may affect oropharynx (tongue, soft palate) or larynx and can be life-threatening Abdominal pain: often associated with nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea and can lead to dehydration and collapse Rash: about one third develop an erythema marginatum rash either before or during an attack. This is non-pruritic and non-urticarial
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Attacks typically peak at 24 hours and resolve over 48–72 hours.**
claims.source_text: Attacks typically peak at 24 hours and resolve over 48-72 hours
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Triggers:** injury (including dental or other surgery), infection, psychological stress, medications (especially oestrogen-containing and ACE inhibitors), menstruation, vigorous exercise, certain foods — or none.
claims.source_text: Can occur spontaneously or may be precipitated by injury (including local trauma, dental or other surgery), infection, psychological stress, medications (especially oestrogen containing and ACE inhibitors), menstruation, vigorous exercise or certain foods
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: Symptoms typically start between 5 and 11 years (40% by age 5) and may worsen in adolescence. **A family history is present in 75%.**
claims.source_text: HAE symptoms typically first occur between 5-11 years of age; 40% experience a first episode by age 5 … The frequency and severity of a HAE attack may worsen in adolescence … Family history of HAE is present in 75% of cases
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Examine the airway:** tongue, soft palate, uvula; laryngeal oedema signs — stridor, hoarseness, drooling, altered voice. **Angioedema behind the teeth is more likely to progress to airway obstruction than angioedema in front of them.**
claims.source_text: Airway swelling: tongue, soft palate, uvula Laryngeal oedema: stridor, hoarseness, drooling, altered voice (ask caregivers) Angioedema behind teeth (eg tongue, posterior oropharyngeal, laryngeal) is more likely to progress to airway obstruction than angioedema in front of teeth
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Redness or itching suggests a diagnosis other than HAE.** Differentials: allergic reactions and anaphylaxis, idiopathic, drug-induced and (exceedingly rare in childhood) acquired angioedema.
claims.source_text: Confirm absence of redness and itching, which would otherwise suggest diagnosis other than HAE … Allergic reactions and anaphylaxis (see Anaphylaxis) Idiopathic angioedema Drug-induced angioedema Acquired angioedema (exceedingly rare in childhood)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Suspected acute attack with no prior HAE diagnosis: check C4.**
claims.source_text: C4 in a suspected acute attack, if no prior HAE diagnosis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: Treating a non-life-threatening attack is at the discretion of the child and parent. **Treatments: icatibant (subcutaneous) or C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate (intravenous).**
claims.source_text: Treatment of any non life-threatening HAE attack should be at the discretion of the child and parent Treatments available are Icatibant (subcutaneous) or C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate (intravenous)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **First line — C1-INH concentrate (Berinert®), any age: 20 international units/kg, rounded to the nearest 500 units, by slow IV injection (4 mL/min).** Symptoms usually stabilise in 30 minutes; a second dose is rarely needed but may be given 30 min to 2 hours after the first (<1% relapse). Do not shake the solution.
claims.source_text: First line C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) concentrate (Berinert®) Given via slow IV injection (4 mL/min) Any age 20 international units/kg, rounded to nearest 500 units Symptoms usually stabilise in 30 minutes Second dose rarely needed but may be given 30 min to 2 hours after first dose (<1% relapse) Do not shake the solution; it may denature the protein
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Icatibant, slow SC injection:** under 12 kg or under 2 years — seek Immunology advice; **12–25 kg 10 mg (1 mL) · 26–40 kg 15 mg (1.5 mL) · 41–50 kg 20 mg (2 mL) · over 50 kg 30 mg (3 mL)**. A second dose can be given 6 hours after the first (<10% relapse); **max 3 doses/24 hours**. Injection-site reactions are usually mild.
claims.source_text: Bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist Icatibant (Cipla) Given by slow subcut injection <12 kg or <2 years Seek advice from Immunology Injection site reactions (usually mild) 12-25 kg 10 mg (1 mL) 26-40 kg 15 mg (1.5 mL) 41-50 kg 20 mg (2 mL) >50 kg 30 mg (3 mL) Any weight Second dose can be given 6 hours after first dose (<10% relapse) (max 3 doses/24 hours)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Airway attack unresponsive to icatibant: give C1-INH concentrate as rescue.**
claims.source_text: In airway attacks unresponsive to Icatibant, use C1-INH concentrate as rescue treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No response after 2 hours: reconsider the diagnosis** and look for other causes.
claims.source_text: Clinical response should be observed within 2 hours. If there is no response after 2 hours, reconsider diagnosis and evaluate for other causes
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Second line, only if the above are unavailable: solvent/detergent-treated FFP** for laryngeal and/or severe abdominal attacks — it may paradoxically worsen angioedema. Consult immunology/haematology, but don't delay in an emergency with no alternative. Adverse effects: commonly nausea, pruritus, rash; rarely allergic reactions, bronchospasm, cardiorespiratory collapse.
claims.source_text: If above treatments are unavailable, consider solvent/detergent treated FFP for laryngeal and/or severe abdominal attacks, though this may have a paradoxical effect and worsen angioedema … Second line Solvent/detergent treated FFP Any age Consult immunology/haematology (don't delay in emergency and no alternatives available) Common: nausea, pruritus, rash Rare: allergic reactions, bronchospasm, cardiorespiratory collapse, fever
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Airway/laryngeal attack is a medical emergency: immediate icatibant or C1-INH concentrate.** Signs of impending obstruction → senior, ICU and anaesthetic involvement, ideally with fibre-optic-guided intubation and surgical airway skills.
claims.source_text: Airway/laryngeal attacks: medical emergency requiring immediate treatment with Icatibant or C1-INH concentrate. Signs of impending airway obstruction should prompt senior involvement/ICU/anaesthetics, ideally with fibre optic-guided intubation and surgical airway skills
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Peripheral swelling:** treat significant pain or disability, or angioedema of the face or genitals; mild swelling that doesn't affect function may not need treatment.
claims.source_text: Peripheral swelling: significant pain +/- significant disability and/or angioedema involving face or genitals should be treated. Mild swelling that doesn't impact function may not require treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Abdominal attack with moderate–severe pain, vomiting and/or distension: give C1-INH concentrate**; consider fluid resuscitation if severe. Mild pain: simple analgesia including NSAIDs.
claims.source_text: Abdominal pain: moderate to severe pain, vomiting and/or abdominal distension require C1-INH concentrate administration. If severe, consider fluid resuscitation. Mild pain can be treated with simple analgesia including NSAIDs
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult the paediatric team:** first episode of swelling or no previous diagnosis · airway/laryngeal attack · no response to medication within 2 hours · relapse after first-line treatment.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric team when First episode of swelling / no previous diagnosis Airway / laryngeal attack No response to medication within 2 hours Relapse to first line treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Transfer:** airway/laryngeal attack (usually needs PICU/HDU observation) · immediately life-threatening situation · care beyond the hospital's comfort level · inadequate response to acute treatment.
claims.source_text: Consider transfer when Airway / laryngeal attack - children will usually require observation in PICU / HDU setting Immediate life-threatening situation A child requiring care beyond the comfort level of the hospital Inadequate response to acute treatment
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge:** after successful emergency treatment, children improving from peripheral or abdominal attacks may go home even if peripheral swelling has not fully resolved. **Every child diagnosed with HAE needs an allergy/immunology consultation.**
claims.source_text: Following successful emergency treatment, children who have started to improve with peripheral swellings and/or abdominal attacks may be discharged even if peripheral swellings have not fully resolved Any child diagnosed with HAE should have a consultation with an allergy/immunology specialist or clinician with expertise in managing angioedema
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Short-term prophylaxis, first line: C1-INH concentrate (Berinert® IV), any age, 20 units/kg rounded to the nearest 500 units, 1–6 hours before any medical, surgical or dental procedure.**
claims.source_text: Short term prophylaxis Medication and administration Age and indication Dosage First line C1-INH concentrate (Berinert® IV) Any age 1-6 hours prior to any medical, surgical or dental procedure 20 units/kg, rounded to nearest 500 units
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Second line, only if first-line prophylaxis is unavailable: icatibant slow SC**, 2 years and over (under 2: seek Immunology advice), under 30 minutes before the procedure; keep an additional dose for emergency and **observe for over 12 hours** afterwards. Doses: under 12 kg seek Immunology advice; 12–25 kg 10 mg (1 mL); 26–40 kg 15 mg (1.5 mL); 41–50 kg 20 mg (2 mL); over 50 kg 30 mg (3 mL).
claims.source_text: Second line (ONLY if first-line prophylaxis is unavailable) Bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist Icatibant (Cipla) Given by slow subcut injection ≥2 years (if <2 years seek Immunology advice) <30 minutes prior to any procedure Additional dose available for emergency Observation >12 hours post procedure <12 kg: seek Immunology advice 12-25 kg: 10 mg (1 mL) 26-40 kg: 15 mg (1.5 mL) 41-50 kg: 20 mg (2 mL) >50 kg: 30 mg (3 mL)

claims.claim: **Long-term prophylaxis** is prescribed by the child's immunologist: oral tranexamic acid, subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (Berinert® SC), lanadelumab or garadacimab.
claims.source_text: Regular medication prescribed by the child's Immunologist to prevent attacks and reduce the burden of disease. Options include oral antifibrinolytics (tranexamic acid), subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (Berinert® SC) and advanced therapies like plasma kallikrein inhibitors (Lanadelumab) and factor XIIa inhibitors (Garadacimab)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency)' (Last updated May 2025), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Hereditary_angioedema_(C1-esterase_inhibitor_deficiency)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Non-acute screening, with an immunologist:** serum C4, C1-INH level and C1 functional assay; **two sets at least 3 months apart**, with at least 1 set after the age of 1 (results are hard to interpret under 1 year). Genetic testing is not usually needed. **Screen the family if confirmed.**
claims.source_text: In the non-acute setting, screening for HAE may be considered, in consultation with an Immunologist: serum C4 level, C1-INH blood level, C1 functional assay Two sets of complement tests should be obtained, at least 3 months apart Genetic testing is not usually required to confirm the diagnosis Both C1-INH levels and function are difficult to interpret in children <1 year of age and at least 1 set of HAE bloods should be performed after the age of 1 If the diagnosis is confirmed, family screening is recommended

claims.claim: **Type 1:** C1-INH function, C1-INH protein and C4 all low. **Type 2:** C1-INH function low, C1-INH protein normal or raised, C4 low.
